title: Induce durable antigen-specific tolerance in autoimmune endocrine disease

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a time-limited treatment that teaches the immune system to tolerate the endocrine tissue it would otherwise attack, with protection persisting after treatment ends. Antigen specificity means directing that tolerance toward the molecular targets involved in the autoimmune disease while preserving useful immunity against infections and other threats. The intended result is sustained protection of endocrine function without unacceptable general immune suppression. This is a proposed capability; the supplied evidence does not demonstrate its achievement.

The broader objective is a transferable approach that can be adapted to more than one autoimmune endocrine disease. Transferability would not necessarily mean administering the same antigen or identical treatment to every patient. As a conceptual distinction, stopping immune destruction and restoring lost hormone-producing tissue are separate tasks: tolerance could preserve surviving tissue or support replacement tissue, but it would not itself establish that an already destroyed gland has been rebuilt.

significance.text: The documented ability of immune intervention to delay progression of type 1 diabetes provides a clinical precedent for changing an autoimmune endocrine disease’s course. The FDA’s 2022 teplizumab approval establishes that narrower achievement. It gives the proposed direction a clinical foundation without demonstrating the durable antigen-specific tolerance envisioned here.

Conditional impact synthesis: if a treatment durably stopped the relevant autoimmune attack while preserving useful immunity, reduced further autoimmune tissue damage would follow directly. Applied early enough, it could preserve remaining hormone production and potentially prevent progression to clinically important gland failure. Applied after disease onset, it could halt additional autoimmune loss, although the resulting clinical benefit would depend on how much functional tissue remained. Successful adaptation across several endocrine diseases would make this a broadly useful therapeutic capability rather than a solution confined to one disease.

Conditional downstream synthesis: tolerance could also protect regenerated cells or replacement tissue against the autoimmune process that damaged the original gland. That protection would address only the autoimmune component of failure. Immune responses against transplanted donor tissue, inadequate cell function, and other causes of graft loss could require separate solutions. Likewise, freedom from hormone replacement would require enough surviving, regenerated, or transplanted tissue to supply the needed hormone; arresting immune attack alone would not establish recovery of a destroyed gland.

missing_breakthrough.text: The proposed missing capability is durable, sufficiently broad disease-specific immune tolerance that produces clinical protection after a limited treatment course, without unacceptable impairment of general immunity. The scientific challenge is to connect a selective immune change to sustained protection of endocrine tissue. A favorable laboratory immune measurement alone would not establish that the destructive disease process had stopped.

Research framing: relevant antigens and disease mechanisms may differ among patients and endocrine diseases, and the targets involved may change over time. These possibilities create concrete design questions: which targets must an intervention cover, how should patients be selected, and how can protection remain effective if the disease response broadens or shifts? The supplied FDA records do not establish this target heterogeneity or its extent. It remains a plausible barrier identified in the research, rather than a biological finding verified by these sources.

Engineering and clinical-development synthesis: an intervention would need to induce the intended tolerance reliably, maintain it after dosing stops, and avoid either renewed autoimmune attack or excessive suppression of useful immunity. Development would also need ways to distinguish a durable tolerogenic mechanism from temporary disease suppression, select treatment timing while protectable tissue remains, and measure tissue function alongside immune effects. These are requirements derived from the proposed capability; the supplied records do not resolve them or establish whether every part of the broader capability remains unmet across all autoimmune endocrine diseases.

current_state.text: On November 17, 2022, the FDA approved teplizumab-mzwv, marketed as Tzield, to delay onset of stage 3 type 1 diabetes in adults and children aged 8 years and older with stage 2 type 1 diabetes. This establishes an approved disease-modifying immune intervention in a defined population. Delaying progression does not establish permanent prevention, durable antigen-specific tolerance, or a cure.

On June 12, 2026, the FDA granted accelerated approval for Tzield to delay decline in endogenous insulin production in patients aged 8–17 years recently diagnosed with stage 3 type 1 diabetes. The letter requires a further adequate and well-controlled trial to verify and describe clinical benefit. Preserving endogenous insulin production in this setting is distinct from demonstrating insulin independence, regeneration of beta cells, permanent tolerance, or efficacy across other autoimmune endocrine diseases.

The approval letter identifies teplizumab as a humanized, Fc receptor non-binding anti-CD3 monoclonal antibody. Its documented mechanism and indications therefore provide a precedent for immune intervention, but these approvals do not demonstrate selective tolerance to the endocrine disease antigens envisioned by this concept. Neither approval establishes a general immune reset across endocrinopathies.

The supplied review reports an untruncated 2022 FDA report and all six pages of the 2026 approval letter, with no recorded extraction issues. The prescribing-information enclosures referenced by the letter were not supplied, so the available material does not support a complete account of dosing, eligibility qualifications, or safety labeling. These limits do not undermine the dated approval statements, but they constrain interpretation of the full treatment conditions.

Evidence-coverage limitation: the supplied search record contains no bounded search entries establishing comprehensive coverage through November 1, 2026. The documented approvals can therefore be described confidently within their dates and scope, while the broader present-day status of durable antigen-specific tolerance across autoimmune endocrine diseases remains unresolved in this record. Missing coverage is not evidence that a relevant result is false or that no additional advance exists.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: controlled studies would show clinically meaningful protection or remission that persists after a time-limited antigen-specific intervention. Protocols should prespecify treatment duration, the period of follow-up after treatment ends, disease-specific clinical and endocrine-function endpoints, and acceptable safety thresholds. No numerical duration or benefit threshold is established by the supplied material; these would need prospective justification for the disease and population being studied.
completion_criteria.label: Clinically meaningful protection persists after time-limited antigen-specific treatment ends

completion_criteria.text: Proposed mechanistic and safety demonstration: clinical protection should be accompanied by evidence of the intended antigen-directed immune change, with assessment of whether protection persists without continuing general immune suppression. Studies should evaluate preserved responses to infections and vaccination and follow participants long enough to assess relapse and delayed harms. Mechanistic evidence would strengthen the explanation of benefit, while clinical outcomes would establish whether that immune change actually protects patients.
completion_criteria.label: Antigen-directed immune change accompanies protection while preserving useful immunity

completion_criteria.text: Proposed breadth and reproducibility demonstration: independently reproduced benefit in more than one autoimmune endocrine disease would provide a convincing test of transferability. Studies should describe the antigens targeted, patient-selection rules, disease stage, residual tissue function, nonresponders, and circumstances in which retreatment is needed. Demonstration in multiple diseases is a proposed criterion for this broader innovation, not an established consensus requirement. Any finite set of studies would establish demonstrated breadth within those populations and conditions, rather than literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Benefit independently reproduced across multiple autoimmune endocrine diseases

completion_criteria.text: Proposed tissue-function boundary: any claim of restored hormone production should separately demonstrate functional surviving, regenerated, or replacement tissue. If tolerance is combined with cell transplantation or regeneration, evaluation should distinguish control of autoimmune attack from the contribution of the tissue-restoration intervention and from other causes of cell loss. A successful immune intervention could satisfy a protection endpoint even when insufficient tissue remains to eliminate the need for hormone replacement.
completion_criteria.label: Restored hormone production requires demonstrated functional endocrine tissue

completion_criteria.text: The 2026 accelerated-approval letter supplies a narrower regulatory precedent for distinguishing an initial authorization from confirmation of clinical benefit: it explicitly requires a further controlled trial. That requirement supports the importance of clinical verification, but does not establish the proposed off-treatment durability, preserved immunity, or multiple-disease criteria above.
completion_criteria.label: Further controlled trial confirms clinical benefit after initial authorization

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison with END-01, “Immune-protected, renewable human islets that restore autonomous glucose regulation”: both concern protecting insulin-producing cells, but END-01 combines a renewable tissue source, graft protection, and functional glucose regulation. END-10 concerns inducing disease-directed immune tolerance. Such tolerance could contribute to protection of transplanted islets against autoimmunity, while donor-directed immunity and other graft-failure mechanisms could still require additional protection.

Conceptual comparison with END-07, “Regenerate a person’s own functional pancreatic beta cells”: regeneration supplies functional tissue, whereas END-10 aims to prevent autoimmune destruction. In type 1 diabetes, a combined approach could pair regenerated beta cells with protection against renewed attack. Neither achievement substitutes for the other, and tolerance alone does not demonstrate beta-cell regeneration.

Conceptual comparison with END-02, “A general platform for replacing failed endocrine glands with feedback-responsive tissue,” and END-08, “Restore ovarian endocrine function without previously banked tissue”: these entries address restoration or replacement of tissue and its endocrine function. END-10 could be complementary where autoimmune attack threatens that tissue. Their broader tissue-restoration goals also encompass problems that antigen-specific tolerance would not resolve.

Conceptual comparison with END-03, “An inexpensive continuous monitor for multiple human hormones,” and END-04, “A predictive theory of interacting endocrine control systems”: measurement and predictive modeling could help characterize endocrine function and responses to treatment. Their principal advances concern sensing and understanding regulation; END-10 concerns changing the immune process responsible for tissue damage. Improved monitoring or prediction would not by itself demonstrate tolerance.

Conceptual comparison with END-05, “Durable, safe resetting of dysfunctional energy-balance regulation,” END-06, “Programmable tissue-selective control of hormone action,” and END-09, “Glucose-responsive insulin that substantially automates insulin dosing”: these approaches respectively address regulatory dysfunction, control of hormone effects, and hormone delivery. END-10 instead targets autoimmune injury to endocrine tissue. Successful tolerance might reduce treatment needs when enough function is preserved, but it would not establish any of these separate regulatory or delivery capabilities.

unresolved_issues: The supplied sources do not establish which endocrine autoantigens must be targeted, how targets differ among patients or diseases, or how often they change over time.
The record does not establish comprehensive status through November 1, 2026, so the broader capability’s present-day unmet status cannot be confirmed from these inputs.
The 2026 approval requires confirmation of clinical benefit; the supplied material does not provide the outcome of that confirmatory trial.
The prescribing-information enclosures were not supplied, limiting assessment of complete eligibility, dosing, contraindications, warnings, and safety conditions.
Appropriate off-treatment follow-up durations, minimum clinical benefits, preserved-immunity measures, and acceptable safety thresholds remain to be defined prospectively.

The extent to which disease-specific tolerance could protect regenerated or transplanted endocrine tissue, and which additional protections would remain necessary, is not established by the supplied evidence.

brief.title: Lasting protection from immune attacks on hormone glands
possible: People whose immune system attacks their hormone-producing glands could receive a limited course of treatment that teaches the body’s defenses to leave those tissues alone. Protection would continue after treatment ends, while defenses against infections remain useful.
The approach could be adapted to different diseases and could also protect replacement cells from the original immune attack.
why: Stopping the attack early could preserve a gland’s remaining hormone production and prevent further loss of function. For people already living with disease, it could protect the tissue they still have.

sources.who: FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research
sources.showed: The FDA approved teplizumab, sold as Tzield, to delay progression to clinically apparent type 1 diabetes in eligible adults and children.
sources.cited_for: Immune treatment can change the course of type 1 diabetes.
sources.not_established: Delaying disease does not establish lasting, target-specific immune tolerance or permanent prevention.

sources.who: FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research
sources.showed: The FDA granted accelerated approval for Tzield to slow loss of the body’s own insulin production in recently diagnosed children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes. A further trial must confirm clinical benefit.
sources.cited_for: Preserving insulin production provides a narrower precedent, with clinical benefit still requiring confirmation.
sources.not_established: The approval does not establish freedom from insulin treatment, lasting immune tolerance, or benefit across other hormone-gland diseases.

shown: Teplizumab has reached approved use to delay progression of type 1 diabetes. This establishes that immune treatment can alter the disease’s course.
It also has accelerated approval to slow loss of insulin production after diagnosis in children and adolescents. That approval requires a further controlled trial to confirm clinical benefit.
missing: Clinical protection that lasts after a limited treatment directed at the disease’s molecular targets ends remains to be demonstrated.
Selective control of the harmful immune response must be linked to tissue protection while useful immunity remains intact.
Independently repeated benefit across different autoimmune hormone-gland diseases remains a requirement for the broader approach.
Stopping immune attack alone cannot establish that a destroyed gland has recovered or that hormone replacement is no longer needed.

milestones.label: Protection persists after treatment ends
milestones.explanation: Controlled studies would have to show meaningful protection after a limited treatment aimed at the disease’s molecular targets ends. This would establish lasting benefit beyond the treatment course.

milestones.label: Selective immune change protects tissue and preserves defenses
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to link protection to immune changes directed at the disease’s targets, with useful infection and vaccine responses preserved. This would connect benefit to selective immune tolerance.

milestones.label: Independent studies reproduce benefit across diseases
milestones.explanation: Independent groups would have to reproduce benefit across multiple autoimmune hormone-gland diseases. This would establish that the approach can transfer beyond a single disease.

milestones.label: Hormone recovery comes from functioning tissue
milestones.explanation: Any claim of restored hormone production would have to demonstrate functioning surviving, regenerated, or replacement tissue. This would distinguish immune protection from recovery of gland function.

milestones.label: A further controlled trial confirms clinical benefit
milestones.explanation: A further controlled trial would have to confirm teplizumab’s clinical benefit after accelerated approval. This would fulfill the narrower requirement to confirm benefit after initial authorization.

uncertain: Which molecular targets need protection, and how much those targets differ or change among patients and diseases, remain open questions.
The necessary follow-up period, minimum benefit, and acceptable effects on useful immunity still need to be defined.
How well immune tolerance could protect regenerated or transplanted tissue, and what additional protection it would need, remains uncertain.

page.title: Antigen-specific tolerance in autoimmune endocrine disease
page.definition: A finite treatment course prevents autoimmune disruption of hormone production by inducing tolerance to autoantigens, the body's own molecules targeted by the harmful immune response. Protection persists after treatment ends, while immunity to unrelated threats is retained.

goal.need: TN-10 established delayed symptomatic type 1 diabetes after immune treatment, with progression still occurring in both groups. In Graves’ disease, antithyroid drugs achieve drug-free remission in about 50% of patients. These outcomes motivate treatment that maintains control of autoimmunity after dosing ends.

figures.caption: TN-10: progression to symptomatic type 1 diabetes
figures.note: Median follow-up was 51 months. Teplizumab is a CD3-directed antibody; these results do not establish antigen-specific tolerance.

completion.title: Endocrine protection persists after antigen-specific treatment ends, with protective immunity retained.
completion.criterion: In an autoimmune endocrine disease, a controlled clinical study demonstrates protection of endocrine function after antigen-specific treatment ends, together with selective control of disease-antigen responses and retained protective immunity, without maintenance immune treatment. Success satisfies the study's prespecified clinical, mechanistic and safety criteria over its registered follow-up. The cited goal documents specify no common numerical duration, effect size or protective-immunity cutoff. Achievement is assessed separately for each disease.
completion.set_by: Atlas provisional operationalization of the NIAID, NIDDK and Immune Tolerance Network goals; no complete external achievement test was found.
completion.basis: Searches of NIAID/ITN definitions, NIDDK planning reports, FDA teplizumab records, DAVIAD objectives and endocrine immunotherapy trials found no complete achievement test for finite-course endocrine tolerance. NIAID allows minimal ongoing intervention and sets no duration. FDA's 2022 approval concerns delayed stage 3 diabetes; its 2026 accelerated approval concerns delayed insulin-production decline at ages 8–17, with confirmation required. This provisional test uses the stated clinical and immune goals without numerical cutoffs.

milestones.title: An antigen-specific endocrine therapy shows laboratory activity and safety supporting human testing.
milestones.criterion: Laboratory pharmacology establishes activity, and product-specific toxicology supports initial human exposure without unreasonable risk. FDA supplies no endocrine-specific numerical cutoff. DAVIAD reported 60–80% suppression of anti-thyrotropin-receptor antibodies versus controls with ATX-GD-459 in a mouse model; the revised ATX-GD-59 formulation had a reported rat no-observed-adverse-effect level above 1 mg/kg. These are consortium-reported results, not peer-reviewed animal datasets; group sizes were not given.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Drug Development and Review Definitions, preclinical development and investigational new drug sections. DAVIAD supplies a Graves’ disease example.
milestones.threshold_quote: reasonably safe for initial testing in humans.

milestones.title: Human dosing establishes tolerability and dose-related risks of an antigen-specific endocrine therapy.
milestones.criterion: Initial human dosing establishes tolerability and dose-related adverse effects sufficiently to support subsequent controlled studies. In the 2019 Graves’ disease study, 12 adults received ATX-GD-59; 10 completed all 10 intradermal doses over 18 weeks. Mild injection-site swelling and pain were the most common adverse events. Five of the 10 completers had free triiodothyronine within the reference interval at week 18; the uncontrolled design does not establish efficacy.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Step 3: Clinical Research, phase 1 purpose and dose-finding description.
milestones.threshold_quote: how much of a drug the body can tolerate and what its acute side effects are.

milestones.title: An antigen-specific endocrine therapy shows preliminary efficacy in controlled human testing.
milestones.criterion: Controlled human studies provide preliminary evidence of effectiveness and characterize short-term risks. BHT-3021 (2013; 80 adults; 12 weekly doses) produced an exploratory week-15 C-peptide change of +19.5% versus −8.8% with placebo at 1 mg (P<0.026), with selective reduction of proinsulin-reactive CD8 T cells. DiAPREV-IT follow-up (28 September 2026; 49 of 50 original children; median 12.9 years) found no overall benefit (HR 1.017, P=0.960); the HLA-DR3-DQ2 subgroup (n=27) had HR 0.315 (95% CI 0.120–0.823). The cited Graves’ study was uncontrolled.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Drug Development and Review Definitions, phase 2 clinical studies. The cited diabetes signals do not establish confirmatory efficacy.

milestones.title: Pivotal testing establishes benefit and an assessable benefit-risk profile for an antigen-specific therapy.
milestones.criterion: Pivotal human testing demonstrates treatment benefit and supplies the safety information needed to assess overall benefit-risk in the intended endocrine disease population. DIAGNODE-3 did not achieve this result: Diamyd’s update of 27 July 2026 reported that its 15-month interim analysis, involving 174 of 321 participants with recent-onset type 1 diabetes, failed the primary efficacy analysis and continuation criteria; the study closed for futility. This result is a company report, not peer reviewed. The cited Graves’ study is phase 1.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Drug Development and Review Definitions, phase 3 clinical studies.
milestones.threshold_quote: evaluate the overall benefit-risk relationship of the drug.

not_found: No complete external achievement test combined off-treatment endocrine protection, antigen specificity and retained protective immunity.
No controlled human Graves’ disease result demonstrating sustained off-treatment antigen-specific tolerance was found.
DAVIAD’s public report did not give animal group sizes for the pharmacology and toxicology results cited here.

results.finding: IMCY-0098: 2 GLP toxicology studies reportedly found it safe in animals; sample sizes not stated.
results.detail: The consortium reports a preclinical proof of concept and regulatory approval for a phase I trial, but gives no specific pharmacology result or toxicology measurements needed to assess the criterion fully.
results.quote: Both toxicology studies confirmed IMCY-0098 was safe in animals.

results.finding: ATX-GD-459 suppressed anti-TSHR antibodies by approximately 60–80% versus controls in mice; group sizes not reported.
results.detail: The revised ATX-GD-59 formulation had a reported rat NOAEL above 1 mg/kg. The consortium reported UK and Belgian trial approvals; Germany requested additional preclinical work. The animal findings are consortium reports, with group sizes unspecified.
results.quote: Prophylactic treatment with ATX-GD-459 in the AdV-TSHR model – efficacy was demonstrated by suppression of the T cell dependent B cell produced anti-TSHR IgG antibodies by approximately 60-80% compared to controls.

results.finding: In 47 adults with type 1 diabetes, 91% of adverse events in the NNC0361-0041 trial were grade 1.
results.detail: The placebo-controlled trial tested four ascending doses. Five grade 3 adverse events occurred, including two in the placebo group; there were no grade 4 or 5 events. The authors concluded that the safety results support further trials.
results.quote: Ninety-one percent of the AEs were grade 1 and primarily confined to abnormal laboratory investigations, including 63 abnormal coagulation results.

results.finding: In 41 adults with type 1 diabetes, 20 experienced injection-site reactions during the IMCY-0098 dose-ranging study.
results.detail: Thirty-one participants were assigned IMCY-0098 and 10 placebo. Adverse events were generally mild; no inferential safety analysis was performed because of the small sample. One serious event at the highest dose was considered possibly treatment-related by the investigator.
results.quote:
Twenty 
patients (48.8%) experienced injection site reactions.

results.finding: BHT-3021 in 80 adults with type 1 diabetes: exploratory C-peptide rose 19.5% at week 15 with the 1 mg dose.
results.detail: In the randomized, placebo-controlled trial, placebo C-peptide fell 8.8%. No serious adverse events were considered related to treatment. The trial was not powered for efficacy, and the C-peptide effect was ultimately lost after treatment stopped.
results.quote:
C-peptide levels improved relative to placebo at all doses, most notably at 1 mg at 15 weeks (+19.5% BHT-3021 versus −8.8% BHT-placebo,

results.finding: In 46 HLA DR3-DQ2-positive participants with type 1 diabetes, GAD-alum treatment had a 1.557 C-peptide preservation effect ratio versus placebo.
results.detail: The randomized trial enrolled 109 participants. Its primary endpoint was not met overall; the subgroup was prespecified before unblinding but the trial was not powered for it. Adverse events occurred in 49% of treated participants and 58% of placebo recipients; injection-site reactions were mild.

results.finding: In type 1 diabetes, sample size not stated, 50% of peptide-treated participants maintained baseline stimulated C-peptide at 24 weeks.
results.detail: The randomized placebo-controlled study provides preliminary efficacy evidence, but the supplied text does not characterize short-term risks or state the sample size.
results.quote: Stimulated C-peptide (measuring insulin functional reserve) had declined in all placebo subjects at 24 weeks but was maintained at ≥100% baseline levels in one-half of the treated group.

results.finding: In 27 HLA-DR3-DQ2-positive children, GAD-alum delayed progression to stage 3 type 1 diabetes (HR 0.315).
results.detail: The randomized trial follow-up found no overall benefit among 49 participants. The subgroup analysis was retrospective and not prespecified in the original trial; multiple testing was not adjusted for. The original trial reported no study drug-associated adverse events.
